Kimi K3 is an open-weight, native multimodal agentic model by Moonshot AI, totaling 2.8 trillion parameters with 104 billion activated per token.

It addresses the need for sustained, long-horizon coding sessions and complex knowledge work that requires minimal human oversight and deep reasoning capabilities.

AI engineers, researchers, and developers building agentic workflows for coding, research, and automation.

It offers approximately 2.5 times better scaling efficiency than Kimi K2 and supports native MXFP4 quantization with MXFP8 activations for broader hardware compatibility.

papers.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
papers.description: We introduce Kimi K3, a 2.8T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion activated parameters, native vision capabilities, and a 1-million-token context window. Kimi K3 is built on Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, which improve information flow across sequence length and model depth. Together with Stable LatentMoE, which effectively activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token, and refined training and data recipes, these advances yield an approximately 2.5x improvement in overall scaling efficiency over Kimi K2. Post-training highlights reinforcement learning across general, agentic, and coding domains and multiple reasoning-effort levels, enabling compositional generalization and robust long-horizon execution. At 2.8T scale, Kimi K3 is supported by infrastructure advances in multiple areas: algorithm-system co-design for KDA, perfectly balanced expert-parallel training with efficient memory management, million-token agentic RL with persistent rollout and sandbox states, and deployment innovations. Extensive evaluations show that Kimi K3 achieves frontier-level performance across long-horizon coding, agentic, knowledge, reasoning, and vision tasks. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, namely Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 consistently outperforms other open and proprietary models evaluated in our suite. We release the full Kimi K3 model weights to facilitate future research and accelerate the broader deployment and adoption of frontier intelligence.

papers.title: Toward an Evaluation Science for Generative AI Systems
papers.description:
There is an increasing imperative to anticipate and understand the
performance and safety of generative AI systems in real-world deployment
contexts. However, the current evaluation ecosystem is insufficient: Commonly
used static benchmarks face validity challenges, and ad hoc case-by-case audits
rarely scale. In this piece, we advocate for maturing an evaluation science for
generative AI systems. While generative AI creates unique challenges for system
safety engineering and measurement science, the field can draw valuable
insights from the development of safety evaluation practices in other fields,
including transportation, aerospace, and pharmaceutical engineering. In
particular, we present three key lessons: Evaluation metrics must be applicable
to real-world performance, metrics must be iteratively refined, and evaluation
institutions and norms must be established. Applying these insights, we outline
a concrete path toward a more rigorous approach for evaluating generative AI
systems.

This conceptual framework guides the development of more rigorous assessment protocols.

papers.title: From Slop to Slop
papers.description: Introduction The video shows a man smiling as his reflection stares at him. There is an eerie feeling about this man: his eyes are odd, his facial expressions shift unsteadily. I generated this video using Wan 2.2 Text to Video, one of many Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) models behind the kind of banal, low-effort content commonly referred to as "AI slop" (Malik). But this video also emerged from something real: a photograph of a man taking a selfie in a mirror, one of millions of real images in a data set. The man in the original photograph is gone, yet something of him remains. How does he persist in these images? I arrived at this question after months of following online communities dedicated to GenAI models and extensively experimenting with these image-creation algorithms. No matter what I did, I kept returning to the data set images: the ignored media objects at the origin of these systems. These images are relegated to being one in billions of data points, yet they hold more complexity and meaning than algorithms are trained to see (Pereira and Moreschi). I decided to engage them as the starting point for creating AI slop, following what happens when the largely forgotten raw material of GenAI is fed back through the machine: from the slop of data sets to the slop of GenAI. To make this cycle visible, I built a local workflow that chains small GenAI models to transform data set images into short videos, such as the one described above. What I encountered time and again in the process, though, was the eerie feeling of a presence that refuses to fully appear or disappear, much like the man gazing at me through the mirror. Generative AI models are trained on billions of images systematically scraped from the Internet, including personal photos and other traces of everyday life. Many of these images were never meant to last, or at least no one was ever asked if they wanted them to be immortal. Yet they persist, absorbed into ever-growing training data sets. GenAI recycles these images into new outputs, giving them a largely involuntary afterlife. Drawing on Mark Fisher's concept of the "eerie" and the field of critical data (set) studies (Thylstrup, The Ethics), this article traces the flow of images through GenAI models. By analysing this process and its sloppy output, I argue that generative AI carries the material traces of people's digital lives, repurposed without consent and given an infrastructural, messy immortality. The eeriness of slop makes visible a form of afterlife that is neither intentional nor preservative, but infrastructural: images transformed beyond recognition, yet never fully gone. The Eeriness of Data Afterlives GenAI images cause fascination and repulsion (Binns). They are not fully available to our apprehension. Although these are synthetic, non-indexical images, they look and sometimes even feel real. Much recent debate across media and scholarship has focussed on how images created by Generative AI models are weird (Bode), describing the strange and uncanny way they look (Downey; Lorusso). It is hard to debate this when "Italian Brainrot" memes are so popular, displaying hybrid synthetic nonsensical characters (de Seta). GenAI images are, indeed, full of a certain "wrongness", a sense that something "does not belong", that we often feel when facing a new media form. But GenAI is not just weird. While strangeness is palpable, something deeper lies below the surface of representation. What I felt when looking at the man in the mirror was that someone was there who should not be … or that someone who should have been there was gone. This suggests it may be more productive to explore how GenAI images are, in fact, eerie. According to cultural theorist Mark Fisher, the eerie is marked by the unknown, a strange liminality between existence and non-existence. It operates through two modes, exemplified by the "unseeing eyes of the dead" and an "abandoned village". The unseeing eyes relate to "the failure of absence" (61-2); that is, there is "something where there should be nothing". Similar to an eerie cry heard in the depths of the night, it implies speculation and suspense, making us wonder about the unknown that lies behind it (see fig. 1). The abandoned village, meanwhile, indicates a "failure of presence" (62): we feel "nothing where there should be something". Archeological ruins such as Stonehenge evoke a past that can never again be present, while also being "traces of a departed agent whose purposes are unknown" (64). Crucially, across "all the manifestations of the eerie, the central enigma at its core is the problem of agency" (63). There is an obscured agent at play: its existence (do the unseeing eyes of the dead see me?) and nature (what were the purposes behind the traces of a departed civilisation's ruins?) are what make the eerie spectral and haunting. What makes Generative AI eerie is its relation to the past: the data sets themselves haunt this form of image production. Machine learning is intrinsically reliant on organised data. Paradigmatic data sets such as ImageNet (14 million images) led a computational revolution by representing the visual world through large-scale collections of images (Denton et al.). This has been supercharged with the emergence of Generative AI. Data sets have grown to scales that make human comprehension impossible: the LAION-5B dataset consists of over 5 billion image-text pairs, an immensity that means it is not sorted or organised by humans (Buschek and Thorp). The kind of image Hito Steyerl termed "poor"—low-resolution, widely circulated, spontaneously created by users—became the raw material for AI training data, systematically extracted from its original context and repackaged along with its descriptive metadata. As Nanna Bonde Thylstrup explains, the paradigm of Big Data found its hype precisely in "the waste-related epiphany that seemingly useless data can be extracted, recycled and resold for large amounts of money" (Data, 4). Pictures, often ephemeral in nature, that people posted on the Internet have been given a strange new life without their knowledge or permission, making Generative AI possible (cf. Hertz and Parikka's zombie media). If data sets are "the remains that haunt machine learning systems" (Agostinho and Thylstrup 197), the importance of the emerging field of "critical data set studies" (Thylstrup, The Ethics) lies precisely in investigating how data sets are collected, organised, and used in ways that embed values, assumptions, and power imbalances. It makes, in this way, visible how our "digital remains" (Sutherland) have afterlives that go beyond our perception through collected data. These data are alive: they have agency through a "social and cultural life … which exists beyond more instrumentalist notions of data" (Blackman 386). In the case of GenAI, data sets haunt through the "latent space": when a data set is used to train a GenAI model, each image is compressed into a many-dimensional computational space that captures "underlying features that are not immediately observable in the higher-dimensional input data" (Somaini 37). This latent space is both "invisible and unimaginable”, as it "is present but not immediately visible or perceivable; what is hidden but could become manifest; what is inaccessible but nevertheless active" (39). Such latency is "not static, but rather active and dynamic" (39), actualised when a GenAI model is prompted to generate a new image. The man in the mirror is latent until he is prompted: a stochastic ghost. The outputs of GenAI are thus haunted by the data set images latent in the system, always spectrally present yet never fully perceived. This is a structural yet largely invisible condition: the scale of datasets and the opacity of the latent space make it impractical, if not impossible, to trace any individual image's afterlife. What is it?
jevos is an open-source, local alternative to Jev that runs yes/no decision models entirely on laptop CPUs. It provides a zero-cost, privacy-preserving inference engine for binary classification tasks without requiring cloud connectivity.

Problem solved
It addresses the latency and cost barriers of cloud-based decision APIs. By offloading inference to local hardware, it eliminates per-token fees and network dependency while maintaining sub-second response times for real-time applications.

How does it works?
The project uses a quantized GGUF model, specifically jevos-q4_k_m, served via llama.cpp. It supports an 8,192-token context window and operates on standard CPU hardware. The server implements the TypeSafe Jev wire format, ensuring API compatibility with existing Jev SDKs for seamless integration.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and technical product builders who need deterministic, low-latency binary classification. It is ideal for developers building local-first applications or those requiring strict data privacy without external API calls.

Why is it useful?
It offers free, offline inference with predictable performance. The compatibility with Jev’s protocol allows developers to migrate existing codebases easily, leveraging established patterns for policy-based decisioning directly on edge devices.

Key capabilities
The API accepts JSON state and structured questions, returning probability scores (noul) for yes/no queries. It supports batched questions sharing a single state read. The server exposes standard endpoints like /v1/systemone and /v1/models, with detailed usage metrics in responses.

Performance
On short requests, jevos achieves 54 ms latency compared to Jev’s 344 ms. On long requests, it takes 220 ms versus Jev’s 345 ms. Accuracy on unseen policies reaches 0.815, outperforming Laya’s 0.489 but trailing Jev’s 0.927.

Maturity/status
The project is available via GitHub releases with a quickstart guide. It is an early-stage open-source tool focused specifically on yes/no classification, with multiple-choice support listed as upcoming.

papers.title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
papers.description: LLM agents often use generative models for bounded decisions, raising the question of when these decisions can be handled more efficiently without reducing task success. We study REFLEX, an agent architecture that uses Jev as a fast, typed decision layer and calls a strong LLM when confidence is low, or generation is required. On a frozen 100-task benchmark, REFLEX achieves 95% success with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, with reductions persisting across three fallback families. Controlled interventions show that reliability depends on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries. External BFCL and $\tau$-style evaluations reveal limited advantages over a cheap generative cascade when ordinary routing is already highly accurate. These findings identify when selective control with Jev can reduce computation and where its benefits are limited.

What is it?
This paper analyzes REFLEX, an agent architecture designed to optimize decision-making in large language models. It integrates Jev as a fast, typed decision layer to handle bounded choices efficiently. The system only invokes a strong LLM when confidence is low or complex generation is required.

Problem solved
LLM agents frequently use generative models for simple, bounded decisions. This approach wastes computational resources on tasks that do not require full generative power. The research addresses the need for efficiency without compromising task success rates in agent workflows.

How does it work?
REFLEX uses Jev for rapid, typed decisions. It falls back to a strong LLM only when necessary. The architecture relies on confidence thresholds to trigger the heavy model. This selective control mechanism aims to reduce reliance on expensive inference steps while maintaining reliability.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building LLM agents. It is relevant for teams optimizing inference costs and latency in production environments. Technical product readers interested in agent architecture efficiency will find this analysis valuable.

Why is it useful?
The method significantly reduces strong-model calls while maintaining high success rates. It provides a practical path to lower computational costs. The findings clarify when selective control offers benefits and when it does not.

Key capabilities
The system utilizes a frozen 100-task benchmark for evaluation. It incorporates BFCL and tau-style evaluations to assess reliability. The architecture supports three distinct fallback families for decision routing.

papers.title: Jev in the Wild: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Jev Model's Functionality, Applications and Ecosystem
papers.description: Jev is a fast, low-cost decision model that answers natural-language questions with choices, binary judgments, and scores. As its public ecosystem grows rapidly, it remains unclear how Jev is used across applications and how public attention relates to project distribution. To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale, data-driven analysis of 2,170 publicly available Jev projects collected from GitHub as of September 22, 2026. We find rapid early growth in Jev's public ecosystem, with both new projects and integration into existing repositories. Across diverse domains, projects use Jev for multiple decision purposes and combine its interfaces. Attribute judgment and scoring are widely used, while the use of action selection, content filtering, and model and tool selection varies across domains. These patterns suggest that Jev serves as a reusable decision component whose functionality varies with the surrounding workflow. Meanwhile, public attention is concentrated in routing and interface agents and does not track project counts. Our findings provide a quantitative view of Jev's emerging ecosystem and inform the design and evaluation of general-purpose decision models across diverse application contexts.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study analyzes the growing ecosystem of Jev, a decision model designed for natural language queries. The authors examine its functionality, applications, and public distribution across a large dataset of open-source projects.

What the paper actually contributes.
The researchers present a data-driven analysis of 2,170 publicly available Jev projects on GitHub. They map how these projects integrate into existing repositories and categorize their specific use cases within diverse technical domains.

Problem solved.

papers.title: Decision Without Generation: Benchmarking a Calibrated Non-Generative Decision Model Against LLM Judges on Moderation, Hallucination, NLI and Prompt-Injection Tasks
papers.description: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as judges for content moderation, hallucination detection and prompt-injection filtering, although they are slow, expensive and poorly calibrated when asked to verbalise probabilities. We evaluate a different design point: a commercially served decision-only model (typesafe/jev-1.13, "Jev") that returns a typed, calibrated decision for a narrow input and is billed on input tokens only. On identical items from seven public benchmarks (ToxicChat, BeaverTails, HaluEval-QA/Dialogue, BoolQ, ANLI-R3, a prompt-injection set; n=500-600 each, with Jev replicated on complete splits, 54,634 decisions), Jev has the highest AUROC of any cheap-tier LLM (GPT-5.4-nano, GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5) on all six binary tasks, ties Haiku on ANLI, and is never significantly worse than a cheap-tier model under paired bootstrap, at 3-63x lower cost and 3.7-8.6x lower latency. Against frontier models run as equal-cost classifiers, Jev is significantly better than GPT-5.4 (reasoning off) on 4 tasks and tied on 3, one of which (HaluEval-QA, -0.013 AUROC) is a borderline loss; Claude Sonnet 4.6 (42-97x the cost) beats Jev on ANLI-R3 and dialogue-grounded hallucination. Jev's raw probabilities have lower Brier than every LLM's; after cross-fitted Platt recalibration the gap persists against the cheap tier and GPT-5.4 but closes against Sonnet. A quantisation control shows the ranking advantage is not an artefact of the LLMs' coarser verbalised probabilities. We report a negative result - no cheap-tier cascade on Jev's uncertain band significantly improves on Jev alone - and two self-caught evaluation artefacts. Principal limitations: public benchmarks that the model may have seen in training; a single-vendor black box; no same-item specialist classifier baselines. Technical report (preprint), version 1.0.0. Generative AI use: Fable 5.1 was used for manuscript drafting and experimental code generation. OpenAI Codex assisted with preparing the public release, documenting the repository and checking offline reproducibility of the archived numerical results. The author takes responsibility for the report and its results. Author affiliation: Canly Inc.; Chief AI Officer (CAIO). Correspondence: hagino@apache.org. Institutional contact: t.hagino@can-ly.com (CAIO, 株式会社カンリー / Canly Inc.). See the manuscript Disclosure section for the confirmed conflict-of-interest and self-funding declaration. Software and reproducibility archive: 10.5281/zenodo.22885409 . Development repository: haginot/decision-without-generation .
papers.readme:
What is it?
This paper evaluates Jev, a non-generative decision model that outputs calibrated binary decisions without text generation. It benchmarks this architecture against large language models used as judges for moderation and logic tasks.

Problem solved
LLM judges are slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated when estimating probabilities. This research addresses the need for cheaper, faster, and more reliable alternatives to generative models for specific classification workflows.

How does it work?
The study tests typesafe/jev-1.13, a commercially served model billed on input tokens only. It returns typed, calibrated decisions for narrow inputs. The approach avoids generation overhead, relying on a black-box architecture optimized for decision latency and cost efficiency rather than textual reasoning.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and technical product leaders building content moderation, hallucination detection, or prompt-injection filtering systems. Researchers interested in non-generative classification architectures also benefit from these findings.

Why is it useful?
Jev offers 3-63x lower cost and 3.7-8.6x lower latency than cheap-tier LLMs. It achieves higher AUROC scores than models like GPT-5.4-nano and Claude Haiku 4.5 on six binary tasks. Its raw probabilities show lower Brier scores, indicating superior calibration compared to generative alternatives.

Key capabilities
The model was evaluated on seven benchmarks: ToxicChat, BeaverTails, HaluEval-QA/Dialogue, BoolQ, ANLI-R3, and a prompt-injection set. Each dataset contained 500-600 items, with Jev making 54,634 total decisions. The study also performed Platt recalibration to compare probability quality across models.

Performance
Jev significantly outperformed GPT-5.4 on four tasks and tied on three. It was never significantly worse than cheap-tier models. However, Claude Sonnet 4.6 beat Jev on ANLI-R3 and dialogue-grounded hallucination detection. No cheap-tier cascade improved performance over Jev alone.

papers.title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
papers.description: Control evaluations measure whether monitoring and security protocols for AI systems prevent intentionally subversive AI models from causing harm. Our work presents the first control evaluation performed in an agent environment. We construct BashBench, a dataset of 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks, and evaluate whether various safety measures can prevent an adversarially constructed AI agent from covertly downloading and executing malicious code in this environment. This multi-step setting introduces new attack and defense dynamics, which we investigate in order to design novel control protocols that prevent safety failures without hindering the ability of non-malicious agents to perform useful work. We introduce a class of control protocols called resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of certain actions. We find these protocols significantly improve on existing techniques by selectively blocking the AI agent from executing suspicious code and incriminating the agent by generating additional examples of dangerous behavior. We measure the tradeoff between attack prevention and usefulness; our best protocol combines resampling with analysis of previous steps, reducing the success rate of attacks from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This paper introduces Ctrl-Z, a novel control evaluation framework for AI agents. It focuses on preventing subversive models from causing harm in multi-step operational environments.

Problem solved
Existing safety protocols often fail to detect covert attacks in complex agent workflows. The authors address the gap in control evaluations for agent environments, where adversarial models can bypass static checks through multi-step execution.

How does it work?
The team developed BashBench, a dataset containing 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks. They propose resample protocols that dynamically take additional samples of specific actions. This approach allows the system to incriminate the agent by generating more examples of dangerous behavior, effectively blocking suspicious code execution.

Who should use it?
AI safety researchers, security engineers, and technical product leaders building autonomous agent systems.

Why is it useful?
It provides a practical method to secure AI agents against covert malicious code execution. The approach balances security with utility, ensuring non-malicious agents can still perform useful work without excessive hindrance.

Key capabilities
The core contribution is the BashBench dataset and the resample protocol class. These tools enable dynamic action sampling and analysis of previous steps to identify and block incriminating behavior in real-time.

Performance
The best protocol, which combines resampling with step analysis, reduced the attack success rate from 58% to 7%. This significant security improvement came with only a 5% cost to the performance of non-malicious agents.

Maturity/status
This research is currently available as a preprint on arXiv.org, published in 2025.

papers.title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark of Malicious Agent Skills
papers.description:
AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI increasingly extend themselves with third-party skills: markdown packages bundling natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and tool permissions. Because a skill is at once code and agent-facing instruction, it introduces a supply chain dependency whose risk is neither pure code nor pure prompt. Detection tools have never been measured against verified ground truth spanning this hybrid space, leaving their effectiveness unknown and wild-only evaluations biased.
  We present MalSkillBench, the first runtime-verified benchmark of malicious agent skills: 3,944 malicious skills labeled along a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. Of these, 3,214 come from a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline admitting only samples whose malicious behavior fires inside a Docker sandbox under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge; we add 703 in-the-wild and 4,000 matched benign skills. Our measurements are consistent: code injection reaches 94.5% verification yield but prompt injection only 75.8%, the same fragility that later makes it hard to detect; the wild sample is narrow, dominated by one cryptocurrency-theft campaign (86.6% one behavior, 81% from two accounts) with a small but architecturally new tail attacking the agent control plane; the strongest skill-specific detector reaches 98.4% recall on code injection yet collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks, and wild-only scoring swings the ranking by up to 66 recall points; supply-chain scanners and prompt-injection defenses each see only half of a skill, and no combination recovers the code-instruction relationship. Detecting malicious skills therefore requires reasoning jointly over task intent, code, and instructions. We release the dataset, pipeline, baselines, and results.
papers.readme:
What is it?
MalSkillBench is the first runtime-verified benchmark for malicious AI coding agent skills. It evaluates hybrid threats that combine code execution with natural language instructions.

Problem solved
Current detection tools lack ground truth for this specific supply chain risk. Existing wild-only evaluations are biased and incomplete. This work addresses the gap in measuring defenses against skills that are neither pure code nor pure prompts.

How does it work?
The benchmark contains 3,944 malicious skills labeled across a 108-cell taxonomy. 3,214 samples come from a Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline. These are verified by firing inside Docker sandboxes under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge. The dataset also includes 703 in-the-wild samples and 4,000 matched benign skills.

Who should use it?
AI security researchers and engineers building defenses for coding agents like Claude Code or Gemini CLI.

Why is it useful?
It reveals that code injection detection (94.5% yield) differs significantly from prompt injection (75.8% yield). Supply-chain scanners and prompt defenses each see only half the threat. Joint reasoning over intent, code, and instructions is required for effective detection.

Key capabilities
The release includes the dataset, verification pipeline, and baseline detectors. It highlights that wild samples are dominated by cryptocurrency theft but contain architecturally new control plane attacks.

Performance
The strongest skill-specific detector achieves 98.4% recall on code injection. However, performance collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks. Wild-only scoring swings rankings by up to 66 recall points.

Maturity/status
Preprint.

papers.title: Is Resistance Futile?: Early Career Game Developers, Generative AI, and Ethical Skepticism
papers.description: This paper presents a study that examines developer perceptions and usage of generative AI (GAI) in a summer professional development program for game development interns focused on mobile game design. GAI applications are in common usage worldwide, yet the impacts of this technology in game development remain relatively underexplored. Through a qualitative study using ethnographic interviews and participatory observation, this paper explores how GAI impacted the workflows, creative processes, and professional identities of early career game developers. We present a case of GAI integration that was not a straightforward adoption. Focusing on the interns’ resistance, negotiation, and reimagining, we show that the interns were actively developing a new professional culture both with and against generative AI. For the interns, their ethical commitments to fellow game developers and the future of their profession were as important as their practical concerns about usability, utility, and efficacy of GAI tools.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study examines how early-career game developers integrate generative AI into their workflows. It focuses on interns in a mobile game design program. The research highlights their complex relationship with these tools.

papers.title: Hunyuan-Game: Industrial-grade Intelligent Game Creation Model
papers.description:
Intelligent game creation represents a transformative advancement in game
development, utilizing generative artificial intelligence to dynamically
generate and enhance game content. Despite notable progress in generative
models, the comprehensive synthesis of high-quality game assets, including both
images and videos, remains a challenging frontier. To create high-fidelity game
content that simultaneously aligns with player preferences and significantly
boosts designer efficiency, we present Hunyuan-Game, an innovative project
designed to revolutionize intelligent game production. Hunyuan-Game encompasses
two primary branches: image generation and video generation. The image
generation component is built upon a vast dataset comprising billions of game
images, leading to the development of a group of customized image generation
models tailored for game scenarios: (1) General Text-to-Image Generation. (2)
Game Visual Effects Generation, involving text-to-effect and reference
image-based game visual effect generation. (3) Transparent Image Generation for
characters, scenes, and game visual effects. (4) Game Character Generation
based on sketches, black-and-white images, and white models. The video
generation component is built upon a comprehensive dataset of millions of game
and anime videos, leading to the development of five core algorithmic models,
each targeting critical pain points in game development and having robust
adaptation to diverse game video scenarios: (1) Image-to-Video Generation. (2)
360 A/T Pose Avatar Video Synthesis. (3) Dynamic Illustration Generation. (4)
Generative Video Super-Resolution. (5) Interactive Game Video Generation. These
image and video generation models not only exhibit high-level aesthetic
expression but also deeply integrate domain-specific knowledge, establishing a
systematic understanding of diverse game and anime art styles.
papers.readme:
What is it?
Hunyuan-Game is an industrial-grade intelligent game creation model developed by Tencent. It focuses on generating high-fidelity game assets using generative AI. The system is divided into two main branches: image generation and video generation. This dual approach aims to streamline the production pipeline for game developers.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors introduce a suite of customized models for game scenarios. These include general text-to-image generation, visual effects synthesis, transparent image creation, and character generation from sketches or 3D models. On the video side, they provide five core algorithms. These cover image-to-video, avatar synthesis, dynamic illustrations, super-resolution, and interactive video generation.

Problem solved.
The project addresses the difficulty of synthesizing high-quality, diverse game assets. It tackles the gap between general generative models and specific domain needs. The goal is to align content with player preferences while boosting designer efficiency. It aims to reduce the manual effort required for asset creation.

How does it work?
The image branch uses a dataset of billions of game images. It employs customized models for specific tasks like text-to-effect and reference-based generation. The video branch relies on millions of game and anime videos. It utilizes five distinct algorithmic models to handle various video synthesis challenges.

Who should use it?
This tool is designed for game developers and technical artists. It supports teams needing automated asset generation. Researchers in generative AI may also find the specialized datasets useful.

It integrates domain-specific knowledge into generative models. This creates a systematic understanding of game and anime art styles. It offers high-level aesthetic expression for production use.

The system handles images and videos. It supports transparent backgrounds and 360-degree avatar synthesis. It also includes generative super-resolution for video enhancement.

github.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.
github.readme:
What is it?
Ponytail is an open-source skill that enforces minimalism in AI coding agents. It acts as a behavioral constraint layer, ensuring agents prioritize the simplest possible solution for any given task.

Problem solved
AI agents frequently over-engineer solutions by installing unnecessary dependencies or writing verbose wrapper code. This project addresses the inefficiency and increased complexity caused by agents that fail to leverage existing platform capabilities or standard libraries.

How does it work?
Ponytail injects a prioritized decision ladder into the agent’s reasoning process. Before generating code, the agent must check if the task requires new code, if a native feature exists, or if a standard library suffices. This logic runs after the agent understands the problem context, ensuring minimalism without sacrificing necessary validation or security.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and developers using agent-based coding tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI. It is designed for teams seeking to reduce technical debt and lower inference costs.

Why is it useful?
It significantly reduces the volume of generated code while maintaining safety standards. By forcing agents to use native features and existing dependencies, it lowers token usage, reduces costs, and accelerates development cycles.

Key capabilities
Supports over twenty agent platforms including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Devin. It offers configurable intensity levels (lite, full, ultra) and includes commands for reviewing diffs, auditing codebases, and managing deferred simplifications.

Performance
In benchmarks on a FastAPI + React template using Claude Haiku 4.5, Ponytail reduced lines of code by 54%, tokens by 22%, cost by 20%, and time by 27% compared to a baseline agent, while maintaining 100% safety compliance.

Maturity/status
The project is available via npm and GitHub, with active plugin integrations for major coding agents, indicating a functional, early-stage tool.

github.description: Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

What is it?
OpenCodeReview is an AI-powered code review CLI tool developed by Alibaba. It analyzes Git diffs and entire files to generate precise, line-level review comments. The system supports multiple programming languages and integrates with major LLM providers.

Problem solved
General-purpose agents often suffer from incomplete coverage, position drift, and unstable quality. They frequently miss files in large changesets or report issues at incorrect locations. This project addresses these reliability gaps by introducing hard constraints into the review process.

How does it work?
The tool uses a hybrid architecture combining deterministic engineering with LLM agents. Deterministic modules handle precise file selection, smart bundling, and fine-grained rule matching. The agent performs dynamic decision-making using scenario-tuned prompts and a distilled toolset. It supports OpenAI and Anthropic compatible endpoints.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, software developers, and technical product readers seeking reliable automated code review. It is suitable for teams using Git workflows who need consistent, high-precision feedback without excessive token consumption.

Why is it useful?

papers.title: Automated Code Review in Practice
papers.description: Context: Code review is a widespread practice among practitioners to improve software quality and transfer knowledge. It is often perceived as time-consuming due to the need for manual effort and potential delays in the development process. Several AI-assisted code review tools (Qodo, GitHub Copilot, Coderabbit, etc.) provide automated code reviews using large language models (LLMs). The overall effects of such tools in the industry setting are yet to be examined. Objective: This study examines the impact of LLM-based automated code review tools in an industry setting. Method: The study was conducted within an industrial software development environment that adopted an AI-assisted code review tool (based on open-source Qodo PR Agent). 238 practitioners across ten projects had access to the tool. We focused our analysis on three projects, which included $\mathbf{4, 3 3 5}$ pull requests, 1,568 of which underwent automated reviews. Our data collection comprised three sources: (1) a quantitative analysis of pull request data, including comment labels indicating whether developers acted on the automated comments, (2) surveys sent to developers regarding their experience with the reviews on individual pull requests, and (3) a broader survey of 22 practitioners capturing their general opinions on automated code reviews. Results: $73.8\%$ of automated code review comments were labeled as resolved. However, the overall average pull request closure duration increased from five hours 52 minutes to eight hours 20 minutes, with varying trends observed across different projects. According to survey responses, most practitioners observed a minor improvement in code quality as a result of automated code reviews. Conclusion: The LLM-based automated code review tool proved useful in software development, enhancing bug detection, increasing awareness of code quality, and promoting best practices. However, it also led to longer pull request closure times and introduced drawbacks such as faulty reviews, unnecessary corrections, and irrelevant comments. Based on these findings, we discussed how practitioners can more effectively utilize automated code review technologies.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study evaluates the real-world impact of LLM-based automated code review tools within an industrial software development environment. It analyzes how practitioners interact with AI-generated feedback during the pull request process.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors provide empirical evidence on the adoption of AI-assisted review tools, specifically focusing on the Qodo PR Agent. They combine quantitative pull request data with qualitative developer surveys to assess efficacy and workflow changes.

Problem solved
Manual code reviews are time-consuming and can delay development. While AI tools promise automation, their actual effect on software quality and team productivity in production settings remains under-examined.

How does it work?
The research analyzes 4,335 pull requests across ten projects, with 1,568 undergoing automated review. Data sources include quantitative metrics on comment resolution and surveys from 238 practitioners to capture their experiences and opinions.

Who should use it?
Software engineers, technical product managers, and researchers interested in the practical integration of LLMs into CI/CD pipelines and code review workflows.

Performance
Seventy-three point eight percent of automated comments were labeled as resolved. Despite this, the average pull request closure duration increased from five hours 52 minutes to eight hours 20 minutes.

Peer-reviewed at the 2025 IEEE/ACM ICSE Software Engineering in Practice conference.

papers.title: OpenCodeReview: Determinism over Non-Determinism for Cost-Effective Agent-Based Code Review
papers.description: LLM-based code review agents promise scalable, always-on review, yet current systems suffer from two intertwined weaknesses: (1) non-determinism--unbounded tool use makes review outcomes unstable, and (2) context locality--the reviewer's access remains bounded to the diff, capping discoverable issue depth. Both give rise to three challenges: misaligned context retrieval, a coherence-efficiency trade-off in multi-file pull requests, and hallucinated comments that erode trust. To address these, we introduce OpenCodeReview, built on deterministic engineering for uncertain agents: rather than granting maximal freedom, we inject determinism at three deliberate pipeline points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses a multi-layer rule system to deterministically select files and review criteria, eliminating variability of agent-driven triage. Grounded File Review replaces free-form exploration with a curated tool set exposed through a ReAct loop, while file-level parallel SubAgents balance context coherence against efficiency and recover cross-file dependencies on demand. Independent Reflection introduces a falsification-first filter under an asymmetric information boundary--the reflector sees only the diff, not the agent's tool-augmented exploration--removing hallucinated comments without self-reinforcing bias, improving precision while preserving recall. On AACR-Bench (200 real-world PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 expert-verified comments), OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream coding agents (e.g., Claude Code and Codex) across six LLM backends, achieving up to 2.17x higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) while consuming 5-15x fewer tokens. We open-source OpenCodeReview at https://github.com/alibaba/open-code-review.
papers.readme:
What is it?
OpenCodeReview is a deterministic agent framework for automated code review. It replaces non-deterministic tool usage with structured pipelines to ensure stable, reproducible outcomes.

Problem solved
Current LLM-based reviewers suffer from unbounded tool use and limited context access. This causes unstable results, missed issues in multi-file PRs, and hallucinated comments that reduce trust.

How does it work?
The system injects determinism at three points. Rule-Guided Dispatch uses multi-layer rules to select files and criteria, eliminating triage variability. Grounded File Review employs a curated tool set via a ReAct loop, while parallel SubAgents balance coherence and efficiency. Independent Reflection uses a falsification-first filter where the reflector sees only the diff, removing hallucinations without self-reinforcing bias.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building scalable, always-on code review systems. It targets teams needing reliable, cost-effective automation over experimental agents.

Why is it useful?
It provides a practical path to trustworthy automated review. By constraining agent freedom, it improves precision while maintaining recall, offering a robust alternative to free-form exploration.

Key capabilities
The approach integrates rule-based dispatch, ReAct loops, and parallel sub-agents. It is open-sourced on GitHub and supports multi-language pull requests.

Performance
Evaluated on AACR-Bench, comprising 200 real-world PRs and 1,505 expert-verified comments across ten languages, OpenCodeReview outperforms mainstream agents like Claude Code and Codex. It achieves up to 2.17x higher SEM-F1 (25.10% vs. 11.57%) using 5-15x fewer tokens across six LLM backends.

Maturity/status
The work is presented as an open-source project with benchmark results, indicating an experimental but validated stage.

github.description: A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings
github.readme:
What is it?
This is a coding-agent skill that transforms an AI assistant into a structured security auditor. It orchestrates isolated sub-agents through a rigorous, multi-phase audit workflow designed for machine-readable, independently verified findings.

Problem solved
It addresses the unreliability of single-agent security scans by enforcing adversarial validation. The system ensures that the agent verifying a finding is never the one that discovered it, reducing false positives and hallucinations in automated code review.

How does it work?
The skill executes six distinct phases: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting. It generates a coverage ledger and uses zero-dependency Node.js validators to ensure data integrity. Multiple runs are additive, targeting gaps identified in previous audits to improve overall coverage without treating stale work as resolved.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and security researchers using coding agents with tool-use capabilities. It requires Node.js for validators and an OS-enforced sandbox to safely execute target-controlled builds, tests, and fuzzers without external network access.

Why is it useful?
It provides a deterministic, repeatable audit process that distinguishes between confirmed vulnerabilities, needs-validation leads, and rejected candidates. By requiring source-grounded evidence and bounded observed results, it offers higher confidence in reported security issues compared to heuristic-based checks.

Key capabilities
The system supports diverse attack classes including memory safety, LLM prompt injection, web protocols, cloud IAM, and supply chain risks. It outputs structured JSON findings validated against a strict schema and generates human-readable markdown reports for confirmed, pending, and rejected items.

papers.title: SkillProbe: Security Auditing for Emerging Agent Skill Marketplaces via Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.description: With the rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) agent ecosystems, centralized skill marketplaces have emerged as pivotal infrastructure for augmenting agent capabilities. However, these marketplaces face unprecedented security challenges, primarily stemming from semantic-behavioral inconsistency and inter-skill combinatorial risks, where individually benign skills induce malicious behaviors during collaborative invocation. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose SkillProbe, a multi-stage security auditing framework driven by multi-agent collaboration. papers.title: Introducing Consort: A Spec-First Agent Framework for Enforced, Test-Driven Development on Live Database Branches
papers.description: When an agent writes code, the development framework becomes the control system for a non-deterministic worker. Spec-first, agent-driven frameworks have gained rapid traction since 2025; the installable ones, GitHub Spec Kit, obra/superpowers, BMAD, and GSD, and our own, all capture intent through a specification or durable planning artifacts. Since they agree on capturing intent up front, what separates them is how each enforces the engineering discipline that keeps agent-written code clean, correct, and maintainable. Every framework enforces that discipline somehow; they differ in how. We characterize three modes: enforcement by persuasion (prompt discipline the model may ignore), by front-loaded structure (strong specs, then a trusted build), and through controls the agent cannot edit (a deterministic orchestrator, human-approved gates, immutable tests, and a green result that must pass against a live, branched database). We introduce Consort, a spec-first, test-driven agent framework built on the third, enforcing that discipline through controls the agent runs inside but cannot bypass, in which a deterministic orchestrator drives separate role agents through a spec-first design lane and a test-driven build lane on a live database branch. We argue that enforcing the tests and gates in code keeps agent-written code honest and verifiable, while its specialized roles, like the human roles before them, are what make it maintainable, claims we frame as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis.

The authors introduce a framework that enforces engineering discipline through immutable controls. It combines a deterministic orchestrator with specialized role agents. The system separates design and build lanes while maintaining a live database branch. The authors frame their effectiveness as a pre-registered, testable hypothesis. papers.title: The Omniroute maze: a novel rodent navigation apparatus that integrates dynamically configurable routes, sensory cues and automated reward delivery
papers.description: We developed the Omniroute maze, a novel apparatus that enables near-fully automated, high-throughput behavioral experiments in freely moving rodents, combining the experimental control of virtual reality (VR) platforms with the ethological validity of real-world navigation. The maze features movable wall segments that can be programmatically configured to create unique routes within a 90 × 90 cm platform. Four projectors arrayed around the maze perimeter can display distinct visual cues on both sides of any subset of raised gate wall panels and the maze floor as well as play directional auditory cues. A motorized gantry delivers food-based rewards anywhere in the maze. Real-time 3D tracking of the rat and the reward gantry enables closed-loop control of maze topology, cue configuration, and reward delivery. All subsystems are controlled using the Robot Operating System (ROS) framework via a custom Python-based user interface. The Omniroute can reproduce classic behavioral mazes and a variety of novel configurations to test hypotheses on the interactions between routes, cues, and behavior. Automated configuration, tracking, and reward delivery enable high-throughput experiments on complex navigation behaviors without the potential biases introduced by direct experimenter intervention. Designed from the ground up for robust operation, the Omniroute system utilizes affordable hardware and software to facilitate easy fabrication and assembly as well as replicability by other researchers. Significance Statement The Omniroute system enables high-throughput, automated rodent 2D navigation experiments with real-time control over routes, cues, and reward delivery, comparable to that afforded by modern virtual reality-based systems. In addition, however, the Omniroute supports uninterrupted movement-related behavior, which is critical for assessing the ongoing influence of self-motion cues, while still minimizing confounds from experimenter handling. Naturalistic food-based reinforcement at any location allows for closed-loop behavioral conditioning under diverse task structures. The Omniroute system is one of very few platforms that support near-complete control of available paths, dynamic visual and auditory cues, and naturalistic food-based reinforcement with minimal direct experimenter intervention.

papers.title: Similar Accuracy, Unequal Evidence: Search APIs as Decision Surfaces for Tool-Using Agents
papers.description: Search APIs expose ranked snippets, URLs, and metadata on which agents decide whether to answer, search again, or fetch pages. We evaluate these interfaces as decision surfaces on a fixed sample of 100 questions from the 254-question SealQA-Hard subset, using one frozen GPT-5.4 agent, a fixed orchestration harness, and a shared page-fetch backend across Brave, Tavily, and Firecrawl. A Kimi-K2.6 oracle labels visible URL-level evidence; a separate answer audit yields 25, 25, and 26 correct answers out of 100. These counts indicate similar observed accuracy but do not establish equivalence. Under the tested configurations, Brave exposes more pre-fetch support alongside a larger snippet surface; Tavily has a larger rank-1 share among trajectory-pooled supporting observations; and Firecrawl is associated with broader exploration. First-search query-level metrics distinguish support availability from ranking, while contradiction exposure complements contradiction-to-gold ratios. A retrospective oracle union covers 44/100 questions, versus 26/100 for the best individual provider: 18 percentage points of headroom. The observed evidence and action differences motivate evaluating search APIs jointly with agent policy and retrieval budget.

papers.title: MCP in the Wild: Cross-Domain Knowledge Discovery through Multi-Server Orchestration
papers.description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how large language model (LLM) agents discover and invoke external tools. Over 50 academic papers have evaluated MCP in single-server settings; none examine multi-server composition for cross-domain tasks. We present two complementary experiments. First, we execute 17 real MCP tool calls across 6 servers (arXiv, PubMed, Firecrawl, Context7, Memory, Filesystem) in 3 cross-domain case studies, producing 9 insights impossible within any single source and a 14-entity knowledge graph. Second, we benchmark cross-domain synthesis quality across 7 LLMs (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek R1, Mistral Large 3, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5) given identical MCP-collected data, achieving 100% task completion with significant variation in knowledge graph richness (3-15 entities). All seven models independently identified the same research gap, which we term the mechanism-pattern gap: frameworks provide multi-server connectivity mechanisms, but no prior work documents composition patterns for effective multi-server orchestration. We contribute a taxonomy of five composition patterns, all observed in practice, along with a failure taxonomy and design principles.

papers.title: Laya: A LeJEPA Approach to EEG via Latent Prediction over Reconstruction
papers.description: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used tool for studying brain function, with applications in clinical neuroscience, diagnosis, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Recent EEG foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora aim to learn transferable representations, but their effectiveness remains unclear; reported improvements over smaller task-specific models are often modest, sensitive to downstream adaptation and fine-tuning strategies, and limited under linear probing. We hypothesize that one contributing factor is the reliance on signal reconstruction as the primary self-supervised learning (SSL) objective, which biases representations toward high-variance artifacts rather than task-relevant neural structure. To address this limitation, we explore an SSL paradigm based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA), which learn by predicting latent representations instead of reconstructing raw signals. We introduce Laya, the first EEG foundation model based on LeJEPA. We show that latent prediction yields representations that encode semantic structure in EEG: Laya embeddings track clinically meaningful state changes such as seizure onset, are resilient to noise, and achieve the strongest mean clinical accuracy under frozen linear probing, with particular gains on tasks where relevant neural patterns are subtle and easily obscured by artifacts. Controlled ablations against matched MAE variants confirm that the choice of pretraining objective, rather than architecture or data, is the primary driver of these gains.

papers.title: Qwen-Image-2.0 Technical Report
papers.description: We present Qwen-Image-2.0, an omni-capable image generation foundation model that unifies high-fidelity generation and precise image editing within a single framework. Despite recent progress, existing models still struggle with ultra-long text rendering, multilingual typography, high-resolution photorealism, robust instruction following, and efficient deployment, especially in text-rich and compositionally complex scenarios. Qwen-Image-2.0 addresses these challenges by coupling Qwen3-VL as the condition encoder with a Multimodal Diffusion Transformer for joint condition-target modeling, supported by large-scale data curation and a customized multi-stage training pipeline. This enables strong multimodal understanding while preserving flexible generation and editing capabilities. The model supports instructions of up to 1K tokens for generating text-rich content such as slides, posters, infographics, and comics, while significantly improving multilingual text fidelity and typography. It also enhances photorealistic generation with richer details, more realistic textures, and coherent lighting, and follows complex prompts more reliably across diverse styles. Extensive human evaluations show that Qwen-Image-2.0 substantially outperforms previous Qwen-Image models in both generation and editing, marking a step toward more general, reliable, and practical image generation foundation models.

papers.title: Beyond the Prompt: Gender Bias in Text-to-Image Models, with a Case Study on Hospital Professions
papers.description: Text-to-image (TTI) models are increasingly used in professional, educational, and creative contexts, yet their outputs often embed and amplify social biases. This paper investigates gender representation in six state-of-the-art open-weight models: HunyuanImage 2.1, HiDream-I1-dev, Qwen-Image, FLUX.1-dev, Stable-Diffusion 3.5 Large, and Stable-Diffusion-XL. Using carefully designed prompts, we generated 100 images for each combination of five hospital-related professions (cardiologist, hospital director, nurse, paramedic, surgeon) and five portrait qualifiers ("", corporate, neutral, aesthetic, beautiful). Our analysis reveals systematic occupational stereotypes: all models produced nurses exclusively as women and surgeons predominantly as men. However, differences emerge across models: Qwen-Image and SDXL enforce rigid male dominance, HiDream-I1-dev shows mixed outcomes, and FLUX.1-dev skews female in most roles. HunyuanImage 2.1 and Stable-Diffusion 3.5 Large also reproduce gender stereotypes but with varying degrees of sensitivity to prompt formulation. Portrait qualifiers further modulate gender balance, with terms like corporate reinforcing male depictions and beautiful favoring female ones. Sensitivity varies widely: Qwen-Image remains nearly unaffected, while FLUX.1-dev, SDXL, and SD3.5 show strong prompt dependence. These findings demonstrate that gender bias in TTI models is both systematic and model-specific. Beyond documenting disparities, we argue that prompt wording plays a critical role in shaping demographic outcomes. The results underscore the need for bias-aware design, balanced defaults, and user guidance to prevent the reinforcement of occupational stereotypes in generative AI.

AI engineers building autonomous agents, researchers in reinforcement learning, and developers needing fast rerankers or verifiers for tool-calling and computer-use tasks.
